claims.text: Advanced machine-learning potentials integrated with enhanced-sampling methods can accurately reproduce solid and liquid free energies near phase transitions.
The proposed workflow can retain vibrational-entropy, anharmonic, and electron–vibration-coupling effects.
The proposed workflow will substantially reduce computational cost relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The proposed workflow will improve throughput relative to TOR-TILD, especially for binary and multicomponent systems.
An MLP can be trained from a sparse set of high-fidelity ab initio free-energy data.
Combining the trained MLP with accelerated molecular dynamics or thermodynamic-integration variants can capture key anharmonic and coupling effects.
The MLP parameterization can reliably interpolate interatomic potentials and free-energy landscapes across solid and fluid phases.
The interpolated representation includes subtle anharmonic distortions and electron–vibration coupling.
The trained MLP provides a continuous and computationally efficient representation of interatomic interactions.
Enhanced sampling with the surrogate model can estimate free energies on both sides of a phase transition while requiring fewer costly ab initio MD simulations.
The workflow will predict free energies within a few percent of explicit ab initio MD benchmarks.
The workflow will reduce computational cost by roughly one order of magnitude.
The workflow will deliver higher throughput than TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems without compromising the required entropy and coupling details.
The workflow is expected to remain reliable from approximately 0.8 to 1.2 times the phase-transition temperature.
The workflow is expected to remain reliable for elemental, binary, and multicomponent systems containing up to five components.
The workflow may be less applicable under extreme conditions with more complex electron–vibration interplay.
